status_summary: No presidential direction to the Office of Federal Procurement Policy and no waiver program for existing contracts was found. The Skills-Based Federal Contracting Act of 2025 (H.R. 5235), which bars minimum education requirements for proposed contractor personnel in solicitations unless the contracting officer gives a written justification, passed the House by voice vote under suspension of the rules on 2026-02-23 and passed the Senate without amendment by unanimous consent on 2026-09-30. The GovInfo bill status record, updated 2026-10-15, lists a message on the Senate action sent to the House on 2026-10-14 as its latest action, with no presentment, signature or public law number. If enacted, the requirement would apply to solicitations issued 15 months after enactment, and the bill does not reach private employers generally.

timeline.event: House passes H.R. 5235, the Skills-Based Federal Contracting Act, as amended, by voice vote under suspension of the rules.
Senate passes H.R. 5235 without amendment by unanimous consent.

title: Adopt skills-based hiring standards for federal contractors
uncertainties: Congress.gov could not be fetched. The GovInfo bill status record was reread on 2026-10-16: its latest action is a message on Senate action sent to the House on 2026-10-14, with no presentment, signature or public law number, and a bill tracker (thelobbynews.com) lists presentment and signature as pending; a web search found no report of signing. The GovInfo record can lag, so a presentment in the days before 2026-10-16 cannot be ruled out, and the ten-day signing period has not been confirmed to have started. The Senate passage is confirmed in the Congressional Record (page S5295). The enrolled text was read in an earlier pass: the restriction allows exceptions with a written justification, requires OMB guidance within 180 days, applies to solicitations 15 months after enactment, and repeals section 813 of the FY2001 defense authorization act. A Federal Register search for degree requirements and contractors returned no executive action; FAR overhaul rules on degree requirements were not specifically searched.
